title: Checkpoint: Defending the Body
objective: After this level you can explain how skin, the immune system and medicine protect us from germs.
summary: Defenses in layers: the skin wall, innate phagocytes and fever, acquired immunity with memory, and human tools. Lymph nodes are where white blood cells fight germs.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: your defenses are built like a castle.
cards.body: A wall, guards on patrol and specialists who remember every enemy, plus a few tools humans added. First, a walk along the walls. Then a stop at the barracks you can sometimes feel swelling in your neck.

cards.headline: Four layers of defense
cards.body: Layer one is the wall: dead, keratin-packed skin cells, replaced about every 4 weeks, on a dry, acidic surface. Layer two is innate immunity, the defense you're born with: phagocytes devour intruders, and fever's heat stirs white blood cells on. Layer three is acquired immunity: B cells, T cells and memory. Layer four is ours. Soap and water scrub germs away, vaccines train memory in advance, and penicillin blocks bacteria from building their cell walls.

cards.fact: Your 'swollen glands' are your immune system at work.
cards.context: Those glands are lymph nodes, part of the lymphatic system from Level 1 that returns fluid and defends against germs. They sit along lymph vessels in places like your neck, armpits and groin. Along with the spleen, they're where white blood cells fight infection, and infections are the most common reason they swell.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How your body defends itself in layers, from the skin wall to immune cells that remember.
Why a fever is your brain turning up its thermostat on purpose to fight infection.
How vaccines train immune memory in advance, and how Jenner's cowpox test gave vaccination its name.
Why antibiotics treat bacteria but not viruses, which multiply only inside living cells.

questions.prompt: Defending the Body recap: what are the 'swollen glands' you can sometimes feel during an infection?

options.label: Blocked sweat glands in the skin
options.rationale: They're lymph nodes, part of the lymphatic system.

options.label: Lymph nodes, where white blood cells fight infection
Mast cells releasing histamine
options.rationale: That's an allergic reaction, not swollen glands.

options.label: Pockets of dead skin cells
options.rationale: Dead skin cells form the outer wall, not glands.

questions.explanation: Swollen glands are lymph nodes; with the spleen, they're where white blood cells fight infection.

questions.prompt: Defending the Body recap: which layer of defense remembers a germ and responds faster next time?

options.label: The skin wall
options.rationale: Skin blocks germs but doesn't remember them.

options.label: Fever
options.rationale: Fever stirs white blood cells but doesn't store memory.

options.label: Acquired immunity, with its B and T cells
Phagocytes in innate immunity
options.rationale: Innate defenses are nonspecific; memory belongs to lymphocytes.

questions.explanation: Acquired immunity keeps memory B and T cells, so a second meeting with the same germ is faster.

questions.prompt: Defending the Body recap: lymph nodes belong to which of Level 1's organ systems?

options.label: Urinary
options.rationale: It filters waste from the blood.

options.label: Integumentary
options.rationale: That's skin, hair and nails, the outer wall.

options.label: Endocrine
options.rationale: It sends hormones that regulate the body.

questions.explanation: Lymph nodes are part of the lymphatic system, which returns fluid and defends against germs.

questions.prompt: Defending the Body recap, from Level 76: what risky practice protected people from smallpox before vaccines?

options.label: Washing in chlorinated lime
options.rationale: That was Semmelweis, in 1847, against childbed fever.

options.label: Penicillin
options.rationale: Penicillin was discovered in 1928, and it attacks bacteria.

options.label: Sensitization
options.rationale: Sensitization is how allergies prime mast cells.

questions.explanation: Variolation exposed people to smallpox material; about 2 to 3 percent died, far fewer than from natural smallpox.

questions.prompt: Defending the Body recap, from Level 74: why does the body raise its temperature during an infection?

options.label: To sweat the germs out through the skin
options.rationale: Sweating comes as a fever breaks, to cool you.

options.label: Heat stirs white blood cells and can slow some germs
Germs are heating the body from inside
options.rationale: The brain chooses the higher setting on purpose.

options.label: To save energy while you rest
options.rationale: Fever costs energy: 10 to 12.5 percent more per 1°C.

questions.explanation: Fever stimulates white blood cells and antibody production, and heat may slow some bacteria and viruses.
